articles.title: Jordan and Iraq block Telegram over national security concerns
articles.summary: Jordan wants to stop ‘attempts to ‌spread extremism’ as Iraq says ⁠app failed to ‘address non-compliant ⁠content’.
articles.body:
Jordanian and Iraqi authorities say they will ban the Telegram messaging app for national security reasons, with Amman saying the move aims to curb the dissemination of illegal content and “extremist material”.

Jordan’s Public Security Directorate (PSD) announced the measure in a statement published on Monday amid a security crackdown after nine people were killed in an attack on a Greek Orthodox church last month.

The PSD urged citizens to “exercise caution when using social media applications, to avoid interacting with accounts, links, or entities of unknown origin, and to report any unlawful practices or content through official channels”.

The church shooting took place in the village of Hammoud in the west-central governorate of Karak. On Sunday, three men were sentenced to death by hanging over the attack.

The incident prompted Jordan to carry out air strikes on neighbouring Syria that Amman said killed more than 20 members of the ISIL (ISIS) armed group linked to the church attack.

Meanwhile, a security officer was killed and another wounded this month in Amman in what authorities described as another “terrorist attack”.

There was no immediate comment from Telegram.

The app, founded by Russian-born entrepreneur Pavel Durov in 2013, is believed to be used by armed groups such as ISIL.

The media and communications authority in Iraq said the blockage was meant to compel Telegram to review Iraqi ⁠content and take measures to prevent violations.

“The operating company failed to ⁠take the necessary measures to address non-compliant content published on the platform and did not adhere to Iraqi laws,” the authority said in a statement.

It gave the company 30 days to comply, without spelling out what would happen ⁠after that.

Iraq also blocked the app in 2023, citing national security concerns and saying it wanted to preserve the integrity of users’ personal ⁠data, which it said the app had mishandled.

Durov, who is believed to be living in exile in Dubai in the United Arab Emirates, faces investigations in several countries. In July, Russia issued an arrest warrant for Durov, accusing him of aiding “terrorism”.

Telegram supports end-to-end encrypted chats, but not all conversations are encrypted. The messaging app is popular in the Middle East and North Africa. The region accounts for about 8 percent of global users.

articles.title: Lebanon’s second airport could provide economic and political benefits
articles.summary: The establishment of a second airport in Lebanon gives the war-devastated country more options for air travel.
articles.body:
Beirut, Lebanon – Lebanon’s second airport is scheduled to begin operating test flights on Independence Day, November 22, in what experts and analysts say could prove to be a boon to the country after years of war and an economic collapse.

In June, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam and other officials took a test flight from Beirut to Rene Mouawad airport, located in the northern town of Qlayaat. Lebanese officials hope a new airport will stimulate growth in one of Lebanon’s poorest and most underserved regions.

Qlayaat airport was originally set to open mid-2026, but Israel’s war on Lebanon delayed it.

The beginning of commercial flights was deferred to November 22, but it was pushed further to mid-December, when many in the Lebanese diaspora return home for the winter holiday, due to construction delays. Commercial flights are now expected to start on December 14.

Rafik Hariri international airport, Lebanon’s only functioning airport, located just south of the capital, Beirut, has been sensitive to political and regional disputes.

Supporters of Hezbollah, the Iranian-backed Shia armed group, have at times weaponised the vulnerabilities of Rafik Hariri airport’s location by blocking the road connecting it to the capital. In February 2025, Hezbollah supporters blocked the road when two Iranian planes were prohibited from landing in Beirut.

A new airport in the north, outside Hezbollah’s traditional zone of influence, could potentially weaken this logistical chokepoint, said Bassel Doueik, a Lebanese political analyst.

“Whenever tensions rise between them and the government, they [Hezbollah] tend to block the inbound and outbound [traffic] on the Beirut airport road through protests, and this is a strategic advantage for the group,” Doueik, a Lebanese political analyst, told Al Jazeera.

“I don’t think the new airport will remove this strategic advantage, but it will actually decrease it to a certain extent because the [Qlayaat] airport is small and it cannot substitute for the current airport.”

Hezbollah has been the strongest military and political actor in Lebanon in recent decades, but its role has come into open debate in the country following the 2024 ceasefire with Israel and the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime in Syria, the group’s key regional ally.

The opening of a new airport is not expected to change internal political calculations, but analysts say it gives the state alternatives in the event of future conflicts.

“The state gains manoeuvrability and alternatives by opening a second airport. But in terms of Hezbollah’s arms or anything else, it doesn’t change much for the state,” Marcel Baloukji, a Lebanese political and security analyst, told Al Jazeera.

“This airport becomes a factor in any potential future war. Beirut airport could be shut down, but alternatives [to fly in and out] would still exist, especially for foreign nationals and diplomatic missions present in Lebanon.”

But officials say the reason for opening a second airport is economic rather than political.

Lebanon’s economy has struggled to recover from the 2019 economic crash due to Israel’s ongoing assault on the country and the US-Israel war on Iran.

Inflation is expected to hit 17.5 percent this year, and the World Bank predicts Lebanon’s economy to contract by 6.4 percent in 2026. Previous estimates suggest Lebanon has suffered damage estimated at more than $14bn since 2023.

Still, Dania Arayssi, assistant director of the New Lines Institute for Strategy and Policy, told Al Jazeera that she believes there is a legislative angle for the establishment of a new airport as well.

“Successfully managing a facility that can generate significant public revenue could help rebuild citizens’ trust in state institutions,” Arayssi said.

“It would show that the government can enforce its authority, protect public assets from Hezbollah’s interference, and lead on delivering services that benefit the country as a whole.”

South Lebanon, where an Israeli invasion has turned into an occupation that analysts believe could last years , has been the worst-affected part of the country as a result of Israel’s war. But other parts of Lebanon are also struggling and have a history of state neglect.

Qlayaat, on the other hand, is located in the northern Akkar region, just 6km (3.7 miles) from the Syrian border. Officials believe the new facility would serve much of Lebanon’s north, as well as important Syrian cities like Homs, Latakia and Tartous, with the northern neighbour struggling to modernise its dilapidated airports.

Experts told Al Jazeera that the fall of President al-Assad in December 2024 partially paved the way for the airport project, as Syria’s former government had been opposed to the idea.

After Salam formed the government in early 2025, plans for the new airport became a priority.

Officials said Qlayaat airport is likely to receive low-cost airlines. In June, Turkiye’s Istanbul and Mersin airports and Dubai in the UAE had been confirmed as destinations for flights from Qlayaat, with new locations likely to be announced in the coming days. Officials said the airport could serve 115,000 passengers in the first year, reaching about 600,000 by the fourth year.

Baloukji said the airport would also have domestic benefits and be a more reassuring route for foreign tourists.

“From the perspective of employing workers, it keeps people in that area and enhances tourism because many people are avoiding Beirut airport due to Hezbollah’s influence,” he said.

articles.title: South Africa shootings: 17 killed in Pietermaritzburg and Pretoria
articles.summary: The shootings in KwaZulu-Natal and Gauteng highlight South Africa's struggle to curb violent crime.
articles.body:
South African police are investigating the murders of 17 people in two separate shootings on Sunday night.

Eight men were fatally shot in a minibus in KwaZulu-Natal province. Police declared them dead when they arrived at the scene. Hours later, nine people were found shot dead inside a shack in western Pretoria.

Police say the two incidents are unrelated. The motive for the shootings has not yet been established.

South Africa is struggling to contain violent crime, including gang-related killings. The country has one of the world's highest murder rates.

Police say they responded to reports of a shooting ⁠outside Pietermaritzburg town in KwaZulu-Natal and found a white seven-seater vehicle riddled with bullet holes.

Inside were eight men with multiple gunshot wounds.

"It has not been established how the incident happened, and police are collecting pieces of evidence to determine the possible motive of the killings and the identity of the suspects," police spokesperson Robert Netshiunda said.

The police have launched a manhunt for the suspects.

In a separate shooting in the Jeffsville informal settlement in Atteridgeville, west of Pretoria, police found the bodies of six men and three women.

They are believed to have been killed inside a four-room shack between 22:00 and 23:00 on Sunday. The bodies were scattered across the rooms, with several spent cartridges discovered outside the shack.

Community members initially mistook the gunshots for thunder and lightning.

"The provincial commissioner of police in Gauteng [province, which includes Pretoria] has mobilized the necessary resources, including the crime intelligence and the deputy provincial commissioner tracking team to search for the suspect," police spokesperson Brigadier Brenda Muridili said.

It's not the first mass shooting in the area. In January, five men were shot dead outside a local shop in broad daylight.

Illegal firearms are widespread in South Africa, where gun violence remains a persistent problem, increasingly involving mass shootings.

In September, 28 people were killed in two separate cases.

Eighteen people were killed when eight gunmen stormed a bar near Johannesburg and opened fire on 25 September. Fourteen others were injured.

In a separate shooting the following day, 10 people were killed outside an entertainment venue in a township near Cape Town. A further 11 were injured.

Much of the violence has been linked to turf wars between gangs involved in drug trafficking and illegal mining.

In February, President Cyril Ramaphosa described organised crime as "the most immediate threat to our democracy, our society and our economic development".

Earlier this year, the military was deployed alongside police to five provinces with the highest murder rates, including Gauteng, in an effort to tackle armed violence.

According to the latest police statistics, 5,427 people were murdered nationwide between April and June 2026, an average of about 60 killings a day. This was a 6% decline compared with the same period a year earlier.

articles.title: Five EU countries announce migrant deportation centre in Rwanda
articles.summary: Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands have announced a "return hub" for failed asylum seekers.
articles.body:
Five EU countries will open a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda next year as part of a broader push to boost removals.

Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands are expected to open a "return hub" ready to accept transfers in 2027, the Dutch and Danish governments announced in statements.

The countries said the scheme would apply to migrants staying illegally in their nations who are subject to deportation, with the Dutch government adding it will provide an alternative if deportees cannot be returned to their country of origin.

Deportees will be able to either integrate into Rwandan society or return to their home country, the nations said.

The scheme will apply to people who have exhausted their legal avenues to stay in the five nations - unlike a scrapped British deal that envisaged sending people to Rwanda to have their claims processed. Legal challenges meant the UK deal never took off, and it was eventually junked by the incoming Labour government in 2024 .

Downing Street has not ruled out the UK joining the scheme, saying they will watch it "with interest".

The five countries say the plan to send migrants abroad is in line with EU and international law, but human rights bodies say it could violate migrant rights.

The deal follows a recent EU reform that allowed for the creation of hubs outside of the bloc.

In a joint press conference in Vienna on Monday, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said the five countries wanted to relieve European asylum systems and stop traffickers arranging deadly trips across the Mediterranean.

In a written statement, the Dutch government said the five countries will "only return single men" as part of the first phase of the deal, adding that the focus for the Netherlands "will be on persons from countries of origin in the same region as Rwanda".

Once in Rwanda, people will be able to integrate into society, which means they will have the right of residence, as well as access to education, healthcare, the labour market and the legal system.

Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta said the country is commmited to working with European partners to provide a "safe, legal and dignified solution for migrants".

He added that they would also work on "correcting the global imbalance in economic opportunities", which he called a "key driver of irregular migration".

Ahead of the announcement, diplomatic sources told the AFP news agency the hub is expected to initially run as a pilot, hosting about 100 people, with each of the five nations possibly sending about 20 migrants.

The United Nations' International Organisation for Migration (IOM) could play an ancillary role.

"IOM has a long history of providing assistance to migrants in situations of transit, including in complex contexts," an IOM spokesperson said, adding the agency was in discussions with some EU countries "on plans for the establishment of return hubs or similar mechanisms".

With elections approaching in several EU nations, administrations have been under pressure to show they can control migration.

Concerns around security, struggling economies and disillusionment with governing parties have all had a major role in shaping attitudes towards people leaving their home countries .

Human Rights Watch's senior Africa researcher Clementine de Montjoye said the choice of Rwanda would be a cause of concern as it had a "well-established record of repression of dissent, arbitrary detention, ill-treatment in detention" and support for armed rebels in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo.

"Paying Kigali to host a deportation programme would not only cause suffering and harm to those deported, it would finance and provide political leverage to a government responsible for serious human rights abuses at home and abroad."

The independent EU Agency for Fundamental Rights argued any third country hosting a return hub should "respect fundamental rights", including that people should not be sent to a country where they face serious risk of persecution.

Unaccompanied children should not be sent to a return hub, the agency said.

According to the European Border and Coast Guard Agency, there were almost 110,000 irregular border crossings into the EU in the first 10 months of 2026, which represents a 29% decrease compared to the previous year.

In October, about 18,100 crossings were detected, which is about 6% less than October 2025 but 22% more than in September "largely because of a sharp rise in arrivals on the Western African route to the Canary Islands".

articles.title: New religious freedom rankings reveal surprising state divide as legal expert warns of costly burdens
articles.summary: Michigan scored just 34% in the 2026 Faith and Freedom Index, ranking last for religious freedom protections affecting faith-based nonprofits.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: Michigan has been ranked last in the nation for legal protections affecting faith-based nonprofits, while Alabama took the top spot in Napa Legal Institute's 2026 Faith and Freedom Index, according to a new report obtained by Fox News Digital that highlights unexpected differences between Republican- and Democratic-led states. The 2026 Faith and Freedom Index, released Monday by Napa Legal Institute, evaluates laws in all 50 states and Washington, D.C., that affect religious organizations, including churches, religious schools, pregnancy resource centers and homeless shelters. The findings, shared with Fox News Digital, show Michigan receiving an overall score of just 34%, followed by Washington at 38% and Massachusetts at 41%. SUPREME COURT OFFERS SUPPORT FOR CATHOLIC PRESCHOOLS CHALLENGING STATE FUNDING REQUIREMENTS Napa Legal senior counsel Frank DeVito told Fox News Digital that Michigan's low score reflects what he described as burdensome nondiscrimination requirements, inadequate religious exemptions and regulatory obstacles affecting faith-based organizations. DeVito said Michigan law can create conflicts for Catholic schools and other religious institutions seeking to make hiring and admissions decisions consistent with their beliefs. He also pointed to financial reporting requirements that he said can impose significant costs on religious nonprofits, potentially diverting resources away from education, charitable services and assistance to vulnerable communities. At the opposite end of the rankings, Alabama led the nation with 80%, followed by Kansas at 76%, Indiana at 75% and Texas at 71%. WASHINGTON FOSTER PARENTS SCORE LEGAL VICTORY AFTER STATE DEMANDED THEY USE CHILDREN'S PREFERRED PRONOUNS But some of the report's most striking findings defy traditional political expectations. New York, a Democratic-led state, scored higher overall than Republican-led North Dakota, South Carolina and Tennessee, while some traditionally conservative states trailed Democratic-led states in certain categories of legal protections. DeVito said New York has stronger exemptions from "nondiscrimination" laws in employment and public programming than Tennessee and that a New York state court ruling found the state's constitution provides greater protections for the free exercise of religion than the federal First Amendment. CATHOLIC NUNS SUE NEW YORK, SAY ASSISTED SUICIDE LAW FORCES THEM TO VIOLATE THEIR FAITH The findings underscore how state laws, not just Supreme Court decisions or congressional legislation, can shape the ability of religious organizations to operate, according to Napa Legal. According to Napa Legal Institute, several states have strengthened protections for faith-based nonprofits in recent years. ONE OF NATION'S LARGEST CHRISTIAN FOSTER AGENCIES WILL NOT ALLOW LGBTQ COUPLES TO ADOPT CHILDREN In Florida, lawmakers updated the state's nonprofit corporation laws to clarify that directors of religious organizations can seek guidance from faith leaders, including priests, ministers and rabbis, when making decisions involving religious matters. Meanwhile, Massachusetts and Rhode Island eased certain financial reporting requirements for nonprofits. Massachusetts increased the annual revenue threshold that triggers a mandatory independent audit for nonprofits raising funds in the state from $200,000 to $500,000, while Rhode Island doubled its audit threshold from $500,000 to $1 million, according to the institute. DeVito stressed the importance of lawmakers establishing lasting legal protections for religious organizations, arguing that churches and faith-based nonprofits provide essential services. VERMONT PAYS $566K IN DAMAGES, LEGAL FEES TO CHRISTIAN SCHOOL IT BANNED FROM ALL SPORTS COMPETITIONS FOR YEARS "For policymakers and government leaders, it's really important to put these laws on the books because the church, the religious organizations do needed work," DeVito said. "They educate children often in poor and disadvantaged circumstances. They feed the hungry, they help the most vulnerable people in society. They do something with the level of love and attention that the government never can." "We need religious organizations to thrive," he continued. "If we are not attentive to the laws being such that these organizations can just do their work rather than spend their time and their money and their resources on administrative burdens that I think are frankly not necessary or fighting lawsuits over, you know, religious liberty issues that they shouldn't have to fight." DeVito warned that burdensome regulations and costly legal battles can divert time and resources away from religious organizations' missions, ultimately hurting society as a whole. He urged lawmakers in both parties to prioritize stronger religious liberty protections, including exemptions from certain nondiscrimination laws and tax requirements, even when doing so presents political or budgetary challenges. articles.title: Pompeii home buried by Mount Vesuvius yields personal treasures untouched for nearly 2,000 years
articles.summary: A woman's cabinet sealed since Mount Vesuvius erupted in A.D. 79 held a children's amulet necklace, perfume bottle, bronze coins and makeup tools, archaeologists found.
articles.body: Archaeologists excavating a home in ancient Pompeii recently uncovered the remains of an ancient Roman cabinet — revealing intimate belongings buried for nearly 2,000 years. The discovery was announced by Pompeii Archaeological Park. Officials said in a press release in late October, which was translated from Italian, that the cabinet was discovered in house IX 11, 7, also known as the House of Cornelius Maximus, along the Via dell'Abbondanza. HIDDEN UNDERGROUND CHAMBER REVEALED BENEATH HOME OF LEGENDARY ROMAN EMPEROR The cabinet — which officials believe belonged to a woman — had apparently remained unopened since Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 A.D. Using clues from the excavation, archaeologists were able to determine what the cabinet originally looked like and identify the belongings stored inside. Pictures released by officials show ancient pottery and other artifacts uncovered during the excavation. The cabinet contained tweezers, a tool for mixing makeup and a glass perfume bottle, as well as an incense burner, a bronze oil lamp and lead weights. SUNKEN ROYAL PALACE WITH CLEOPATRA LINK YIELDS RARE FIND TIED TO LONG-LOST WONDER OF ANCIENT WORLD Among the discoveries was a necklace made up of at least 24 miniature charms, including depictions of gods, hands, feet, pine cones and bunches of grapes. Such necklaces, known as crepundia, were given to Roman children as protective amulets. They also made noise as children moved, which allowed adults to hear them. Officials believe the owner may have retained the necklace as a childhood keepsake. "Adults sometimes kept these objects, often in small boxes or, as in this case, in cloth bags inside cabinets, evidently as reminders of a childhood of which little else sometimes remained," officials said. ANCIENT BURIAL REVEALS RARE JEWELRY FIND THAT ARCHAEOLOGISTS CALL 'HIGHLY UNUSUAL' Archaeologists also discovered a small hoard of 38 bronze coins, though the denominations were not specified, leaving their monetary value unclear. "The presence of the coins, in particular, suggests that the female owner or owners did not have time to retrieve their possessions of economic or sentimental value," officials said. "We cannot reconstruct with certainty the identity of those who lived in the house, but these fragments bring us closer to their everyday lives." The inhabitants of the residence may have fled during the eruption but never returned to recover their belongings, unlike others who apparently returned to dig for their possessions, according to evidence from recent excavations. "But perhaps they did not survive. ... These are questions destined to remain unanswered," the release added. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Gabriel Zuchtriegel, director of Pompeii Archaeological Park, said in a statement that the objects found at the excavation site "bring the human dimension of the past back to life." Said Zuchtriegel, "We cannot reconstruct with certainty the identity of those who lived in the house, but these fragments bring us closer to their everyday lives." The excavation also revealed elaborate wall paintings inside the home, suggesting its residents were relatively well-off. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Construction work was underway when Mount Vesuvius erupted, however, which may have disrupted daily life in the home. Archaeologists also found the skeletons of at least two young mice inside a storage vessel on a mezzanine level. The excavation also revealed elaborate wall paintings inside the home. The mice were likely wood mice, which commonly make their way into homes looking for food — a reminder that ancient Romans dealt with unwanted household pests, much like people today. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The find is one of many discoveries made at Pompeii in recent years. Earlier this year, archaeologists uncovered 2,000-year-old love notes etched into a wall, using advanced imaging technology to reveal inscriptions that had long gone unnoticed. articles.title: Minneapolis renters say they kept paying rent while their landlord accumulated more than $1 million in unpaid city utility bills across five properties; the city has now moved to collect the money through property taxes
articles.summary: Tenants in Minneapolis are questioning their rent payments as their landlord, Fine Associates, amasses over $1 million in unpaid utility bills, prompting city action to recover the debt through property taxes.
articles.body: Tenants at five Minneapolis properties owned by Fine Associates say they have continued paying rent despite the landlord accumulating more than $1 million in unpaid city utility bills. The outstanding balances include water, sewer and rubbish charges, prompting the city to take steps to recover the money through property taxes.Minneapolis has recorded a sharp rise in overdue utility payments, with an 892-page city document listing more than $12 million in unpaid balances. Fine Associates is among the landlords with the largest outstanding debts, according to city records cited by FOX 9 News.The issue has also drawn attention to complaints from residents who say maintenance problems and delayed repairs have affected their buildings.Minneapolis moves to recover more than $12 million in unpaid billsThe Minneapolis City Council voted on Thursday to transfer delinquent utility accounts to Hennepin County, allowing the outstanding amounts to be added to property tax bills.City officials estimate that 98% of these charges are typically paid through the process. Accounts that remain unpaid could eventually lead to foreclosure.Two downtown apartment buildings owned by Fine Associates account for a substantial portion of the company's outstanding balance. One property owes approximately $500,000, while another has accumulated $363,000 in unpaid utility charges."We have a downtown apartment building that owes the city half a million dollars, and another downtown apartment building that owes city $363,000," Minneapolis council member Linea Palmisano told FOX 9 News.City records show that Fine Associates owes more than $1 million across five properties.Tenants question where their rent payments are goingResidents at Marquette Place and 110 Grant have formed tenant unions and taken legal action against Fine Associates, alleging unsafe living conditions and delays in essential maintenance.Some tenants say the unpaid utility bills have raised further questions about how their rent is being used, particularly when residents believe their payments already cover services such as water."We're receiving invoices, we're paying our rent. So where is that money going?" Hannah Crippen, a resident at 110 Grant West, told the news outlet.Minneapolis council member Elizabeth Shaffer also raised concerns about landlords collecting rent that includes utility costs without paying the corresponding bills."If renters are paying, you know, included in their rent is their water bill and the landlord is not paying the water bill, you know, that's definitely a little bit of a slush fund for them," Shaffer said.Residents also claim communication with the landlord about building problems has been limited, with many disputes moving into legal proceedings. During the court process, tenants said Fine Associates had documented hundreds of thousands of dollars in repairs.Residents report flooding and delayed maintenanceTenants at the properties have described recurring problems, including flooding and water damage that they say has sometimes remained unresolved for days or months.At 110 Grant West, residents also point to the closure of the building's swimming pool as an example of maintenance delays."For example, the pool has not been operational since August 2025. But they keep saying, or throughout our lawsuit, they kept saying that it was like days away from opening," resident Blythe Baird told FOX 9 News.Despite their complaints, residents say they value the community they have built and want the properties to receive the maintenance they believe is needed."You know, this is a great place to be, and they could make it and continue to have it be a great place to be," Crippen said.You use AI every day. articles.title: Spain's Canary Islands flooded by thousands of migrants as country declares emergency
articles.summary: Spain's Canary Islands processed over 2,200 migrants in two days as violent protests over housing costs and skyrocketing rents erupted nationwide.
articles.body: Thousands of migrants flooded Spain's Canary Islands this weekend as the nation's government remains under a migration emergency. The Canary Islands have received the brunt of migration from West Africa and Sub-Saharan Africa in recent months. Authorities there processed over 2,200 migrants in just two days, all arriving in dinghies and makeshift boats. One flotilla of 14 boats landed on the island of El Hierro carrying 1,324 people. The island's Spanish population is just 12,000. SPANISH JOURNALIST SAYS CEUTA RESIDENTS BELIEVE GOVERNMENT ISN'T DOING ENOUGH TO PREVENT ANOTHER MIGRANT RUSH The Spanish government declared an emergency over the archipelago last week. The latest surge comes just months after tens of thousands of migrants crossed into Spain's North African territory of Cueta in July. The country also faced internal unrest this month after a general strike turned violent last week and rioters began clashing with police, setting fires and bashing storefronts in hotspots across the country. WOMAN, 87, DIES AFTER BEING CARRIED FROM HOME OF 70 YEARS ON STRETCHER DURING EVICTION IN SPAIN Violent scenes unfolded in Barcelona, where some demonstrators vandalized stores along the city's popular Paseo de Gracia shopping boulevard, set small bonfires and launched fireworks at officers arriving in riot gear and armored vehicles. The violence erupted as Spain experienced its first general strike in 14 years, with workers demanding relief from skyrocketing rents and the rising cost of living. TOURIST HOT SPOT FACES HOUSING REVOLT AS LOCALS DEMAND CUTS TO VACATION LODGING Housing activists claimed 400,000 people marched through Barcelona, while city officials estimated attendance at 55,000. Government officials reported another 120,000 demonstrators gathered in Madrid despite heavy rain, The Associated Press reported. The nationwide walkout disrupted public transportation, forced some businesses to close and blocked major roads. Police made arrests across the country, while officers used pepper spray against demonstrators in Madrid. articles.title: Houthis edge closer to Aden as Yemeni forces pull out of Bab al-Mandeb
articles.summary: Houthis edge closer to Aden as Yemeni forces retreat from the Red Sea coast, threatening global maritime security.
articles.body:
Forces aligned with the internationally recognised Yemeni government face a potentially catastrophic situation, as Houthi forces advance on the southern city of Aden and other strategic areas.

Yemeni government forces said on Sunday they had withdrawn from Dhubab airport and territory they held near the Bab al-Mandeb strait, southwest of Yemen, to defend Aden, the de facto seat of the government.

Retired Lebanese Brigadier-General Hassan Jouni, a military and strategic expert, said fighting is now focused on control over a mountainous triangle of territory in southern Yemen, which could decide the outcome of the war.

This area links Aden to Taiz, another city held by the government but encircled by the Houthis – an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God) – and Bab al-Mandeb, a maritime chokepoint that connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.

“This triangle is the strategic centre of gravity for the war in Yemen as a whole,” Jouni told Al Jazeera.

On Sunday, government-aligned forces were withdrawn from Dhubab, which was recaptured from the Houthis in September, to avoid an imminent siege in the coastal strip by the Houthis and to help defend Aden, analysts say.

Houthi advances in this southwestern region now threaten to completely cut off the government’s coastal supply routes, Jouni said.

The Yemen war began when the Houthis, a Zaidi Shia group close to Iran, captured the capital, Sanaa, in September 2014, forcing the government to flee south to Aden. Saudi Arabia launched an Arab coalition military campaign to aid the government in March 2015, launching thousands of air strikes against Houthi forces.

Following a relatively peaceful few years, fighting re-erupted in July when government forces’ jets bombed Sanaa international airport to prevent a Houthi delegation from landing in the Yemeni capital.

A Houthi offensive in September saw the government lose control of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including the key port city of Mocha . Later Houthi advances also saw Taiz completely besieged by the Houthis.

Yemeni Armed Forces spokesperson Majed al-Nuzaili defended the retreat from Dhubab, saying it was part of a wider tactical manoeuvre.

“[The redeployment] is an extension of the heroic positions of the popular resistance and the southern forces in protecting the temporary capital Aden,” he said on X.

But Jouni believes the situation faced by government forces is grim, with the Houthis reaching Tor al-Baha, just 80km (50 miles) from Aden.

“The Houthi forces have reached this line, meaning that they are indeed in the defensive line area of the city of Aden. We do not say they have approached Aden, but the defence of the city of Aden begins in this area,” he told Al Jazeera.

“The basic combat direction now is in the vicinity of the besieged city of Taiz. On the other hand, of course, the Houthis will focus their attention now on approaching Aden and controlling the first defensive zone.”

Strategic affairs expert Ali al-Dahab gave a less optimistic assessment of the situation than the one presented by the government.

“What happened is a retreat or a withdrawal with the same meaning, and not a redeployment, because the withdrawal left a vast vacuum filled by the Houthis,” al-Dahab stated.

The government’s “Operation Yemen Dawn” has responded to the situation with a dramatic increase in strikes on Houthi positions, including 900 targeting operations within 24 hours.

The Houthis have responded with ballistic missiles and drone attacks towards Mecca, Riyadh, and the Eastern province in Saudi Arabia. They have announced they will continue operations under a principle of “siege for siege, airport for airport, and escalation for escalation”.

Al-Dahab said this strategy is directed at Saudi Arabia, the Yemeni government’s key international ally, and not at authorities in Aden.

With their recent gains on the coast along Bab al-Mandeb, which has become increasingly significant to global maritime trade since the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz amid the US-Israel war on Iran, the Houthis have significant geopolitical leverage.

“They now directly and completely control the western Yemeni coastal sector and part of the maritime extension towards Aden,” al-Dahab warned.

“The matter translates the Houthis’ gains in Bab al-Mandeb in large part to the benefit of Iran.”

articles.title: Jobs at risk at Worcestershire County Council due to AI
articles.summary: An AI tool is set to be used to replace 22 social care jobs.
articles.body:
An AI tool could be used to help replace more than 20 jobs that are being axed at Worcestershire County Council, with bosses warning deeper staff reductions are on the way.

The authority is consulting over cutting 22 full-time equivalent roles in children's and adult social care, with artificial intelligence being relied on to pick up the administrative workload.

The move has been criticised by the union Unison, which said it was "deeply concerned" about "automation" replacing humans.

Councillor Adam Kent, the deputy leader, said: "This isn't a way of removing staff; it's a way of transforming services - it massively improves productivity and accuracy."

The council wants its staff to use an AI-powered transcription tool called Beam Notes, effectively an online note-taker that automatically turns records of meetings into structured reports.

The tool has been developed specifically for frontline public sector workers like NHS staff, housing officers and social workers.

Under the policy, social care workers who deal with vulnerable children and adults would use it to transcribe in-person and online meetings.

A report on the move argues it would "speed up assessments", reduce the amount of admin involved and potentially free up 20% to 30% of a social worker's time.

Beam Notes is already in use elsewhere in the public sector, including at councils in Swindon, Kingston, Dundee and Hampshire.

The authority has been battling a financial crisis for several years and is facing a black hole of £98m next year unless it makes drastic changes.

As recently as August, independent assessors warned the council's finances were in severe trouble unless it drove through radical reforms.

The council's leadership - a coalition of Green, Liberal Democrat and independent councillors - is working on a "transformation plan" aimed at addressing the problems, which includes proposals to scrap the equivalent of 100 jobs.

The drive towards AI is part of that strategy, with a report in April suggesting the work of 63 people could be saved if the council were to rely more on the use of AI assistants.

In June, the council's chief executive, Paul Robinson, went further and told a scrutiny meeting that AI would take over "process-driven" tasks in multiple roles across the council, potentially freeing up roughly one in 10 people.

The authority's political leadership is keen to move swiftly, now that local government reorganisation has been delayed until 2029.

Unison has responded angrily to the job reductions in social care, saying the roles at risk are "critical to safeguarding".

The 22 job reductions have been revealed in a consultation document that the union is currently examining.

A Unison spokesperson said: "While administrative roles are often described as support functions, they are critical to safeguarding, care management, statutory compliance, financial administration, case management, record-keeping and the efficient delivery of services to vulnerable children, families and adults.

"The assumption that digitalisation, automation and process redesign can absorb the loss of experienced staff requires robust evidence and meaningful consultation with those who undertake the work daily."

But Kent told the BBC he believed AI would reduce human error and speed up internal processes.

He also said he considered Beam Notes "safer" than relying on human record-keeping.

"Broadly speaking, AI will increase productivity and accuracy. We are going to see it in every working environment," he said.

"AI will become massively important; it will be a game-changer for councils and businesses well into the future.

"With children's and adult services, for example, it will ensure accurate note-taking and allow people to be much more productive and efficient.

"It's a technology. We used to use typewriters before people had computers; we used to have a horse and cart, and then we had a car.

"This is change. You either accept change and go along with it, or you ignore it - and if we ignore it, it'll cost residents more money."

In Hampshire, 1,800 social workers now use Beam Notes, with the council estimating that 3,000 staff days have been saved and productivity has risen by 20% over the last year.

articles.title: "Brasil está desbordada, los de Ancelotti juegan mal en defensa y ataque"
articles.standfirst: Fernando Kallas analizó en La Tribu el mal momento de la selección brasileña, explicó que la marcha de Davide Ancelotti ha afectado al grupo
articles.summary: Fernando Kallas analizó en La Tribu el mal momento de la selección brasileña, explicó que la marcha de Davide Ancelotti ha afectado al grupo
articles.body: El periodista Fernando Kallas analizó en La Tribu de Radio MARCA el mal momento de la selección brasileña, explicó por qué cree que la marcha de Davide Ancelotti ha afectado al grupo y destacó los dos golazos de Vinicius ante Japón. Fernando Kallas dejó un diagnóstico contundente sobre el momento de Brasil en La Tribu de Radio MARCA. El periodista señaló los problemas de juego de la selección de Carlo Ancelotti y la dificultad del equipo para mantener la calma cuando el partido se complica. "Hay muy mala sensación en este momento en relación al trabajo de Ancelotti en Brasil", aseguró. El amistoso ante Japón le sirvió para explicar por qué. El conjunto japonés ya ganaba 2-0 a la media hora y, a juicio de Kallas, dejó al descubierto las carencias de la selección brasileña. «Es un equipo que juega mal en defensa, juega mal en ataque. Un equipo que emocionalmente y anímicamente está totalmente desbordado», afirmó. El periodista puso como ejemplo el nerviosismo de Ancelotti con el arbitraje. "En un amistoso con Japón, demuestra que ya empieza a sentir la presión". Kallas también apuntó a un cambio en el cuerpo técnico. Según explicó, las personas cercanas a la selección con las que ha hablado atribuyen a Davide Ancelotti un papel importante en los entrenamientos y en la gestión del grupo. "La marcha de Davide ha dejado a este equipo un poco sin mando", resumió. El periodista amplió el foco a la formación de futbolistas en Brasil y habló de una "crisis generacional". A su juicio, selecciones como España, Francia y Portugal se benefician de una cultura de cantera más consolidada. En Brasil, Kallas echa de menos la aparición de centrocampistas y cree que buena parte del talento joven se concentra en una misma posición. "Todos los talentos que salen de Brasil son extremos", sentenció. Kallas sí destacó el papel de Vinicius, autor de dos goles ante Japón. Además de la calidad de las dos acciones, el periodista valoró la respuesta del jugador del Real Madrid con el partido cuesta arriba. "Se echó el equipo a la espalda. Tuvo actitud", explicó. Para Kallas, esa capacidad de rebelarse cuando peor pinta el partido es una de las señas de identidad del brasileño. "Vinicius, cuanto peor, mejor para él. Parece que saca las fuerzas", apuntó. En plena discusión sobre su momento en el Real Madrid, Kallas ve en la actuación ante Japón una oportunidad para que el delantero recupere confianza.

articles.title: ‘My arms are empty’: Tragedy strikes Gaza family after baby dies from cold
articles.summary: A nine-month-old baby has died from hypothermia inside his family’s displacement tent in Gaza, as winter returns.
articles.body:
Khan Younis, Gaza Strip – For Susan Arqiq, the hardest part of the day comes at night, when the noise around her fades and she is left alone with the absence of her nine-month-old son, Kinan. She is still struggling to understand how the cold took his life.

Susan, 26, had put him to sleep beside her on Wednesday night, as she had done countless times before, at their camp in Khan Younis. When she woke in the early hours of the morning to change his diaper, she found Kinan’s face blue, his hands stiff and his body cold.

Her arms, which had held him through countless nights, are now empty.

“My son was pressed against the tent’s tarpaulin. The bedding was still damp,” she told Al Jazeera.

“I switched on my phone’s flashlight and found that his face was completely blue, his hands were stiff, and his body was like ice. My heart nearly stopped from fear. I immediately woke my husband. I was screaming, ‘Kinan, Kinan!’ I could not understand what was wrong with him.”

Her husband did not speak. He picked up the baby and, accompanied by men from the camp, rushed him to hospital.

Women from neighbouring tents, woken by the cries, gathered around Susan. They tried to reassure her that her baby would be all right, but the news from the hospital confirmed her fears.

Kinan died on Thursday, November 12, after a severe drop in his body temperature, according to medical sources. His death was the first cold-related fatality recorded in Gaza during the current winter season.

Susan and her husband, Ahmed Arqiq, 33, have been in shock since the tragic death of their son. Ahmed says Kinan had no known health problems before that night.

“At the emergency department, they told me, ‘May God compensate you. The child has died, and the cause is the severe drop in temperature,’” Ahmed says. “I was shocked… My heart is broken, and even now I cannot believe it.”

Israel’s war on Gaza, which began in October 2023, has seen at least 73,600 Palestinians killed and large parts of the occupied Palestinian territory reduced to rubble. Due to the destruction of their homes or Israeli military occupation, around 1.4 million people are living in tents or makeshift displacement camps.

Israel’s siege on Gaza has prevented mobile homes, tarpaulins, and other essential materials from entering the territory.

The Arqiq family are one of many living in a worn-out displacement tent in the al-Mawasi camp near Khan Younis in southern Gaza as winter approaches. The shelter offers little protection from the cold or the rain, which flooded camps across Gaza during a storm last week.

Ahmed has been unable to find work since the war, and they struggle to afford even the basic necessities of life.

“I have struggled to obtain adequate shelter, blankets, clothing and food for my children. My life is all about suffering,” he said. “Look at my tent. We live in poor conditions. During the last winter storm, we were flooded with water.”

Ahmed said the family had not received a proper tent or tarpaulin to protect them from the winter weather before Kinan’s death. After Kinan died, they received the waterproof sheet, but it was too late to protect him.

Kinan was the youngest of three children, and his brothers, Rami, three, and Ali, two, were deeply attached to him. They continue to ask about their younger brother, unable to understand why he is no longer with them.

“They always ask where he has gone. Whenever they see his belongings, they try to look for him. It is unbelievable,” Ahmed said.

Kinan’s death has renewed fears among displaced families in Gaza as winter sets in. Last week, heavy rain and flooding battered displacement camps across Gaza, damaging tents and leaving families exposed to cold and wet conditions. At least four children died in the floods.

Babies are particularly vulnerable to hypothermia as their bodies are less able to regulate temperature, especially when exposed to cold for prolonged periods.

At least 11 babies are believed to have died due to the cold in Gaza last winter.

Hadeel al-Midana, 27, lives in a displacement tent west of Gaza City with her three children: Hamza and his two older brothers, Mahmoud, seven, and Nour al-Din, five. Her husband, Ibrahim, has been out of work since the war.

She said Kinan’s death has deepened fears she carries each night when she tries to keep her own youngest son, one-month-old Hamza, warm.

“I am always on edge. I cannot leave him,” she told Al Jazeera.

The family struggles to keep the children warm with limited clothing and blankets.

“I swear, he doesn’t have a blanket of his own. I wrap him in the blankets that I use myself,” Hadeel says, referring to Hamza.

The family has received second-hand clothes from neighbours. They were also provided with four blankets at the camp, but Hadeel said the cold inside their tent remains difficult to endure.

“Even the adults cannot bear it. How much worse is it for the little children?” she asked.

She wakes up several times during the night to check on Hamza. Two nights ago, she found his hands and feet were as cold as ice. Terrified, she covered him with a thicker blanket.

She says she needs more blankets for her baby and a small bed to lift him off the ground.

“I need blankets for him, and perhaps a bed that would raise him a little above the ground. I am afraid of the insects, too,” she said.

“The tent is not fit for a child’s life, or even an adult’s life. We live in constant fear, and there is nothing we can do to face it. I hope we get through this winter safely.”

Susan Arqiq sits beside her baby’s belongings, still struggling to comprehend how the cold took the life of her nine-month-old son, Kinan [Abdelhakim Abu Riash/Al Jazeera]
Susan Arqiq looks through her son Kinan’s belongings in her family’s tent [Abdelhakim Abu Riash/Al Jazeera]

articles.title: At least 17 killed in two South Africa mass shootings
articles.summary: Eight men killed in shooting near Pietermaritzburg while six men and three women shot dead near Pretoria.
articles.body:
At least 17 people have been killed in two separate mass shootings in South Africa, police said.

Eight men were found dead late on Sunday in a “bullet-riddled” vehicle in Sweetwaters, outside the city of Pietermaritzburg, police said.

Hours later, nine people were found dead in Jeffsville, an informal settlement near South Africa’s capital, Pretoria, police said. The bodies of six men and three women were discovered inside a shack with gunshot wounds.

National Police Commissioner Fannie Masemola said on Monday that investigators had not established motives for the crimes that took place 530 kilometres (330 miles) apart.

“The ongoing mass shootings which we encounter are unacceptable. Definitely, we have to find these criminals. We cannot allow them to terrorise communities or determine how people live their lives,” Masemola said.

South Africa has struggled for years with high rates of violent crime, but has had a recent surge in mass shootings with high death tolls.

Reporting from Pretoria, Al Jazeera’s Clement Manyathela said the community was “gripped by fear” as it waits for answers about the shooting.

He said the victims were found in a four-room shack, where the killings happened just before midnight. A young child who went into the shack looking for a relative made the discovery, he said.

Pathologists, investigators and officers were working to establish what happened.

Gauteng Police Commissioner Tommy Mthombeni said one of those killed was a “person of interest” in a shooting last year in the nearby informal settlement of Saulsville, in which 12 people were killed and 13 wounded, the Associated Press news agency reported.

“We cannot rule out that they may be linked, and may possibly have been a retaliation attack,” Mthombeni said.

In the Pietermaritzburg shooting, police spokesperson Robert Netshiunda said some families had come forward to help identify victims.

“It’s still too early to tell what the motive could have been and who could be behind the shooting because we are yet to identify the victims,” said Netshiunda.

articles.title: David Chadwick confirmed as new leader of Welsh Liberal Democrats
articles.summary: The 34-year-old's confirmation as his party's leader comes just two years after he became an MP.
articles.body:
David Chadwick has been confirmed as the new leader of the Welsh Liberal Democrats.

The 34-year-old became MP for Brecon, Radnor and Cwm Tawe two years ago, and takes over from the party's only member of the Senedd Jane Dodds, who stood down after nine years in charge.

With only one elected representative in the Welsh Parliament and one in the House of Commons, Chadwick was the only person eligible to stand.

On Monday, Chadwick said he wanted to "lead the Welsh Liberal Democrats into the next chapter of our history", promising to rebuild the party as a "political force capable of shaping the future of Wales".

Jane Dodds standing down as Welsh Liberal Democrats leader

In his first speech as leader at St David's Hotel in Cardiff, he admitted the party had lost ground in communities where they had previously seen success.

"This year's Senedd elections showed how much work remains to be done. But we should never confuse our recent electoral results with the limits of what we can achieve," he said.

"I want us to rediscover the ambition of a party that competed for parliamentary seats across Wales, led cities like Cardiff, Wrexham and Swansea, and was a serious force in communities from north to south."

Chadwick, who was elected as an MP in 2024, told the audience in Cardiff that becoming the party's leader in Wales was not something he could have imagined 10 years ago.

It was around then he had survived a near fatal car crash and developed a rare illness that had left him completely paralysed.

"I went from being a healthy, independent young man, travelling the world and planning my future, to being entirely dependent on others. It changed my life," he said.

"It taught me how quickly any of us can find ourselves needing help, and how much our futures can depend on the care and support available to us."

Chadwick's first challenge as leader is next May's local elections. Currently, the party runs Powys council in a coalition with Labour.

Although he acknowledged that they would be "very tricky", Chadwick told Radio Wales' Sunday Supplement programme that his target was to "take full control of a couple of councils", and to see the start of a recovery in other councils across Wales.

"We will rebuild in communities where we've lost ground, and establish ourselves in places where we've never been strong".

Dodds, who was made her party's Welsh leader in November 2017, will continue to represent the constituency of Brycheiniog Tawe Nedd in the Senedd.

But after a disappointing Senedd election where the Liberal Dems failed to increase on their members in the Senedd, she said "building that team will take years of hard work in communities across the country, and I believe that work should be led by a new generation".

Relations between Dodds and the UK Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey were strained after he previously called her leadership into question.

Chadwick said that Sir Ed was "supportive of us growing the party in Wales" and that he "looked forward to inviting him to Wales sometime soon".

articles.title: After the US aviation shutdown triggered mass cancellations, analysts estimate the four largest airlines face a combined $345 million earnings hit; more than 18,500 flights had been cancelled by Monday morning
articles.summary: America's four biggest airlines could face a combined $345 million loss in earnings after a nationwide aviation shutdown grounded flights and caused more
articles.body: America's four biggest airlines could face a combined $345 million loss in earnings after a nationwide aviation shutdown grounded flights and caused more than 18,500 cancellations by Monday morning. The estimate comes from brokerage firm Bernstein, according to Reuters. The disruption began on Friday afternoon, 13 November 2026, when the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered all departures across the United States to stop temporarily because of a technical failure.Although flights started moving again later that evening, the disruption continued to affect airline schedules throughout the weekend. Data collected for Reuters showed that more than 18,500 flights travelling within, into or out of the United States had been cancelled by 8:47 am Eastern Time on Monday, 16 November. The four airlines facing the biggest financial impact are American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and Southwest Airlines. The carriers lost money from cancelled tickets while also facing high costs to move stranded aircraft and flight crews back into position.Uneven recovery across major carriersAll major US airlines faced schedule problems over the weekend, but some took longer than others to get their operations back to normal. According to a research note from Bank of America analysts cited by Reuters, American Airlines and JetBlue Airways faced the biggest operational problems on Sunday. American cancelled 22 per cent of its Sunday flights, while JetBlue cancelled 28 per cent. The figures were much lower for other major carriers. Delta cancelled 5 per cent of its Sunday flights, Southwest cut 4 per cent and United cancelled 3 per cent. Investors also reacted to the disruption. JetBlue shares fell around 4 per cent in early trading on Monday before recovering some ground and reducing their losses to less than 2 per cent, according to Reuters and Quartz. Shares of the four largest US airlines also fell slightly in premarket trading. However, they later rose by between 1 and 2 per cent on Monday morning.How a single router triggered a nationwide haltThe travel disruption began at around 3:30 pm Eastern Time on Friday, when the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop. The restriction remained in place until 8:15 pm. More than 3,500 aircraft were already in the air when the order was issued. However, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed that all the flights landed safely. Federal officials said over the weekend that the problem was linked to older communications equipment and not a cyberattack. According to the FAA, older hardware became unstable after its network received a large number of data requests, reaching 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds.Officials said on Saturday that the failure may have started with a single router installed by aerospace and defence company L3Harris. Following these disclosures, L3Harris shares fell around 4 per cent in premarket trading on Monday. During a news conference in Washington on Saturday, reported by CTV News, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford explained why the agency decided to stop flights. "What we saw was instability. We couldn't explain the instability. We saw the instability start to propagate into facilities we couldn't identify," Bedford told reporters. "That's when we made the decision to ground stop out of our abundance. No facilities went dark. Nothing was fully boxed."Bedford also explained how the problem spread through the network. He said the network pressure "overwhelmed one set of routers in an in-facility, which then went through the backups at other facilities, and it propagated from there." The FAA said on its website that technicians took immediate steps to prevent another failure. They disabled the affected function on the routers where the problem started. They also switched off the same feature on around 60 similar routers across the network.Political fallout and funding demandsThe nationwide shutdown soon attracted attention in Washington, with officials facing questions about whether recent government technology upgrades had contributed to the failure. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy rejected suggestions that the FAA's artificial intelligence-powered SMART system was responsible. Speaking at a White House briefing reported by Quartz, Duffy said SMART "isn't plugged in" to the live air traffic control network. During an appearance on ABC's "This Week" on Sunday, Duffy said the wider economic impact of the shutdown would probably run into billions of dollars. He also used the incident to call on Congress to provide more funding to replace and improve the country's ageing air traffic control system. Duffy said on Sunday that the government needed to identify the exact "root cause" of the router failure before making major changes. He also pointed out that the FAA could not simply cancel its existing contract with L3Harris.Passenger rights and the return to normalFor tens of thousands of passengers left stranded by the disruption, the weekend meant long queues at airport customer service desks and hours spent waiting on the phone to speak with airline representatives. Since the ground stop was ordered by federal regulators rather than caused by the airlines, US rules do not require carriers to pay for passengers' hotel stays, meals or cash compensation. However, passengers whose flights were cancelled are still entitled to a full ticket refund under US Department of Transportation rules if they decide not to accept another flight offered by the airline. Major carriers also introduced temporary travel waivers. These allowed affected passengers to change their travel plans without paying additional fees. By Monday morning, airline schedules had largely returned to normal. American Airlines said in an update issued on Sunday night that it was ready to operate a mostly normal schedule on Monday. articles.title: Photos: Highlights from Pope Leo’s historic, 12-day tour of South America
articles.summary: They turned out in their millions to greet Pope Leo as he made his way around Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on a gruelling 12-day tour of the South America.
articles.body: LIMA, Peru — They turned out in their millions to greet Pope Leo as he made his way around Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on a grueling 12-day tour of the South American nations, weeks after undergoing successful surgery for lung cancer. For some — particularly those in Argentina, which had not received a papal visit since Pope John Paul II in 1987 — it was the first time they would get to see a pontiff in person. A record 2.5 million people flooded onto the streets of Buenos Aires last week to try and catch a glimpse of Leo. The Vatican dubbed it a “homecoming” tour for the 71-year-old, as the Chicago-born pontiff, who is also a citizen of Peru, spent the final six days in the country where he lived for decades and served as a bishop until 2023. NBC News takes a look at some of the highlights from his trip. Montevideo, Uruguay After a 17-hour flight from Rome, Leo and his entourage touched down in Uruguay’s capital, Montevideo. Praising the Lord and thanking his wonderful medical assistants, Leo said that while some had questioned whether he would be able to make the trip because of his recent surgery, he “had no doubt and was convinced that this trip had to go forward.” Paysandu, Uruguay An estimated 40,000 people waited patiently for Leo, who traveled more than 450 miles from Montevideo to Paysandu, a riverside economic hub in Uruguay’s northwest. Many stood outside overnight, braving the rain. Drawing inspiration from the nearby General Artigas International Bridge, which connects Uruguay and Argentina, Leo told the crowds that bridges bring “openness, communication and exchange.” Florida, Uruguay, and Buenos Aires After celebrating an outdoor Mass with around 50,000 people in front of the National Shrine of Our Lady of the Thirty-Three, the cathedral basilica of the Uruguayan city of Florida, Leo traveled to Argentina’s capital. It was a trip his predecessor, Pope Francis, was never able to make, even though he came from the country. After meeting with President Javier Milei, Leo called on the country’s political leaders to “safeguard democracy” and demonstrate a “careful use of words” in his first speech in the country. Buenos Aires An estimated 2.5 million people turned out to Leo’s first Mass in Argentina at Buenos Aires’ Monumento a los Españoles, the Vatican said, his biggest liturgical event to date. Again, thousands waited overnight hoping for a good spot. Before he greeted the throngs, however, Leo made a pilgrimage to the Cottolengo Don Orione in the south of the city which is home to more than 400 people with disabilities. Cordoba, Argentina After flying to Argentina’s second most populous city, Leo met with bishops, priests and other members of the clergy at the Cathedral of Our Lady of the Assumption where he recalled the teachings of Francis about the poor. “Even those who have the least can teach us a great deal,” he said. Buenos Aires and Lujan, Argentina On a visit to the Villa Devoto Federal Penitentiary in Buenos Aires, Leo urged prisoners to use their time as an “opportunity to begin your lives anew.” The pontiff celebrated another huge Mass to a crowd of 2 million outside the shrine of Our Lady of Lujan, Argentina’s most important Catholic site, before he left the country for Peru. Lima, Peru On an emotional return to the South American country where he served as a missionary for two decades, Leo was greeted by an estimated 3 million people, the largest crowd of his papacy. In a closely watched speech to President Keiko Fujimori, he urged her to confront the wounds of the country’s turbulent past, alluding to the contested legacy of her father and presidential predecessor, Alberto Fujimori, who was in office from 1990 to 2000 and later convicted of human rights abuses. He was pardoned in 2017 and died in 2024. Chiclayo, Peru On a triumphant return Friday to the city of Chiclayo, where as Robert Prevost he served as bishop for eight years and was affectionately nicknamed “Padre Roberto,” Leo said it was a blessing to be in his adopted home exactly one month after he underwent lung cancer surgery, an operation which many feared would force him to cancel the trip. “As I look at your faces, a prayer of thanksgiving to the Lord arises in my heart for the blessing you have been and continue to be in my life,” he said, as the crowd, estimated by the Vatican to have been 1.5 million people, cheered in the Pampas de Pimentel, a desert plain to the west of the city. Santa Cruz de Succhabamba, Peru After boarding a military helicopter, Leo flew to a remote corner of his former diocese to hold an open-air Mass in the Andean highlands. Acknowledging that many in the 20,000-strong crowd had a much more difficult journey than him, he told them the journey that they made was “not only a passage along difficult roads, but also a pilgrimage of faith.” Pucallpa, Peru After approximately 100,000 people took part in the meeting at the Saqsaywaman National Archaeological Park, Leo was greeted by a largely Indigenous audience in the Peruvian city of Pucallpa, an eastern gateway to the Amazon, about 124 miles west of the Brazilian border. There, he condemned deforestation in the world’s largest rainforest and pollution caused by oil and gold production. “Many Indigenous leaders have been murdered for defending their territories,” he said, “The blood of these brothers cries out to God and demands justice.” Lima, Peru After meeting staff and residents at shelter for the Little Sisters of the Abandoned Elderly, a religious institute dedicated to the care of older people, Leo will hold a short ceremony at the Callao Air Base in Peru, before he departs for Rome, where he will arrive Tuesday morning. Claudio Lavanga reported from Lima, Veronica Sanchis Bencomo from New York, and Max Butterworth from London.

articles.title: Iran braces for natural gas shortages during winter energy imbalance
articles.summary: The gas infrastructure in Iran has suffered from underdevelopment and sanctions, and now damage from the war.
articles.body:
Tehran, Iran – Iran is heading into winter with warnings of natural gas shortages, as damage from strikes by the United States and Israel deepens an energy imbalance that has plagued the resource-rich country for years.

Iran holds the second-largest proven natural gas reserves in the world, only behind Russia, but its government last week forecast a peak-demand deficit of about 430 million cubic metres per day for winter that could impact both households and industries.

The country’s ageing energy infrastructure has long suffered from underinvestment and international sanctions that have restricted finances and equipment. Authorities say that inefficient consumption and limited storage capacity are also to blame, in addition to the damage from the ongoing war.

Saeed Tavakoli, head of the National Iranian Gas Company, told local media last week that 26 projectiles struck six refineries on March 18, knocking out 28 percent of Iran’s gas production capacity in the immediate aftermath of the strikes.

According to the government, about 100 million cubic metres per day of processing capacity has since been restored, but fully bringing back the additional 130 million cubic metres lost in the US and Israeli attacks could extend into 2028.

Hashem Oraee, head of the Iranian Energy Associations Union, told local media last week that Iran was not able to rely on any gas imports to plug the gap.

Gas shortages could also lead to electricity blackouts if the gas feeding some power plants goes out, something that has repeatedly happened in recent years. To avoid electricity shortages, those power plants resort to burning cheap fuel , predominantly a heavy oil alternative called mazut, which significantly pollutes the air.

Despite that, Mostafa Rajabi Mashhadi, a deputy energy minister, told the state-linked ILNA outlet on Saturday that mazut burning would continue this year.

Umud Shokri, energy strategist and senior visiting fellow at George Mason University, said that if the problems facing Iran’s gas industry remain unresolved over the coming years, the consequences would extend beyond the energy sector, affecting industrial production, employment, inflation, and living standards.

“In my view, Iran’s biggest challenge is not a lack of energy resources, but its inability to turn those resources into reliable supplies for its people and economy,” Shokri told Al Jazeera. “Without serious reforms, sustained investment, and better energy management, what is now largely a seasonal crisis could gradually become a year-round problem.”

Gas accounts for 73 percent of Iran’s energy mix, the gas company’s Tavakoli said last week, adding that household consumption had reached 480 million cubic metres per day and was expected to sharply rise as the cold season approaches.

Last winter’s peak consumption for households, businesses and small industries was recorded at 737 million.

The National Iranian Gas Company identifies 11 of Iran’s 31 provinces as considerably vulnerable to shortages this winter, particularly some provinces to the north of the country, including Mazandaran, Golestan and North Khorasan. High consumption due to cold temperatures, as well as locations near the ends of transmission lines, increase gas pressure problems in those provinces.

Government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani explicitly warned during a press conference last week that if consumption grows, gas might be cut off across the country, including Tehran.

“Unlike electricity, which can be reconnected quickly after being cut off, bringing back gas after cutoff is a time-consuming process,” she said. “So, network stability is of utmost importance and we must work to prevent any disruptions.”

The government has said it will do its best not to let households or industries go offline due to gas shortages. But on Saturday, the Zagros Petrochemical Company, operating in southern Iran’s energy production hub of Asaluyeh, notified its shareholders that it shut down a methanol production unit until further notice in line with directives from the National Iranian Gas Company

David Jalilvand, managing director at Orient Matters, a geopolitical research consultancy in Germany, said the industrial sector would bear the brunt of the shortages as the authorities prioritise households, which rely on gas for heating.

“Prioritising households, however, does not guarantee that residential supplies will remain uninterrupted if shortages become severe,” he told Al Jazeera.

To help save on gas, the government has tasked its affiliated executive bodies with reducing their gas consumption by 20 percent. It has also said offices are obligated to keep their temperatures at around 18 degrees Celsius (64 degrees Fahrenheit), while homes are advised to maintain 18-21C (64-70F). Offices must also switch heating off on holidays.

The government said inspections last week led to disconnections at the Education Ministry building and five other government buildings in Tehran that were not complying with the energy-saving directives.

The government has also been struggling with a lingering petrol supply imbalance, and imposed sporadic power blackouts to cover electricity production shortfalls during summer and early autumn. In addition to raising the price of petrol twice in less than a year, the government has also significantly limited monthly petrol quotas allocated to personal vehicles.

Authorities have repeatedly asked Iranians to help offset the shortages by consuming less, while saying more price hikes are possible over the coming months.

An October directive also required eligible civil servants to work from home at least two days a week and encourage commuting without private cars on one day a week, as part of efforts to reduce fuel consumption.

“We must speak to the people honestly and explain we are facing gas shortages due to previous years’ imbalances and also damages from the war, so we need to save on gas,” First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref said last week.

High-consuming users have also been told their gas prices will increase exponentially if they do not reduce consumption.

Jalilvand, from Orient Matters, said developing the South Pars gasfield , the world’s largest offshore natural gasfield shared between Iran and Qatar, has been cruicial in addressing the key challenge of keeping the supply of gas growing in line with domestic demand.

But he said sustaining production growth increasingly depends on addressing technical challenges that require foreign investment and technology.

“An equally important challenge lies on the demand side. Iran has enormous potential to improve energy efficiency, but realising it requires investment, technology and domestic policy reforms, particularly to address heavily subsidised energy prices.

“Reintegration into the global economy would make it considerably easier to finance and implement these improvements.”

Hamed, who runs a small apartment hotel in the northern province of Mazandaran, said his business experienced a drop in gas pressure last year, depsite not being a heavy consumer. But there were no total cutoffs.

He told Al Jazeera that lower-pressure gas can impact his business by affecting heating in guest rooms, disrupting the boiler for hot water used for showers and sanitation, and most of the hotel’s kitchen operations.

“It’s basically everything; I really hope it doesn’t come to that this year,” he said.
