articles.title: Elderly homeowner’s hired help turns into squatter nightmare made worse by blue state laws: report
articles.summary: Jordy Smith, 76, said a fake plumber locked her out of her San Diego home and rented rooms to over a dozen people before Squatter Squad intervened.
articles.body: An elderly woman said a man posing as a plumber took over her home in California and began renting it out to more than a dozen people – many of them appearing to be homeless. The situation had been brewing for more than two years before law enforcement finally removed the group after blue state laws complicated the issue, according to the homeowner and those helping her. Jordy Smith, 76, opened up about the situation that took over her life in the City Heights neighborhood of San Diego, where she reportedly hired this man to repair pipes. He then allegedly locked her out of the home and was renting it out to a revolving door of people, according to KGTV. ALLEGED MALIBU SERIAL SQUATTER FEATURED IN NEW DOCUSERIES AFTER YEARS OF HOMEOWNER COMPLAINTS Smith told a reporter that she temporarily moved from her home after she broke a hip and invited the unnamed "plumber" to make the repairs while she was gone. "He just took over and, like, before we knew it, there was like 15 people," she said. HOW THE 'SQUATTER HUNTER' IS FIGHTING HOME TAKEOVERS WITH TECH In a post on social media, Squatter Squad, which is a "squatter removal and prevention" company that was hired to remove the group, said, "Boats were showing up. RVs were moving onto the property. More people were staying there. The contractor had started inviting others onto the property, renting out rooms and even charging people for RV space." Smith said she later discovered the man was not a licensed plumber and had transferred the home’s utility accounts into his name before allegedly beginning to rent out rooms to others. NYC LANDLORD PLEADS FOR HELP AS '9-YEAR-SQUATTER' CONTINUES TO DRAIN HIM DRY IN COURT SAGA: 'TWILIGHT ZONE' She and her partner found themselves locked out of their own home. "I couldn’t sleep at night. I mean, it just seemed like we’d never get back home," she said. SAN FRANCISCO HOME WITH HISTORY OF SQUATTERS UNDER CONTRACT FOR $1.3 MILLION Attempts to confront the people living inside reportedly went nowhere, with Smith saying occupants would lock the door and refuse to speak with them. Squatter Squad told KGTV that squatter issues are "often treated as civil matters," making it difficult for homeowners to remove them. LEE GILLEY BEGS FOR ITALIAN PROTECTION AS ALLEGED SQUATTER TARGETS HOME WHERE PREGNANT WIFE WAS KILLED Under California law, if squatters continuously reside on a property for 30 days, they legally acquire "tenant-at-will" rights. SUPREME COURT REJECTS MICHIGAN FAMILY'S CLAIM THAT COUNTY COMMITTED 'HOME EQUITY THEFT' OVER $2,200 TAX DEBT Once this 30-day threshold is reached, law enforcement treats the situation as a civil landlord-tenant matter rather than criminal trespassing, meaning police cannot simply remove the occupant, and the property owner must go through the formal legal eviction process to regain possession. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X In a statement sent to Fox News Digital, Lando Thomas, owner of Squatter Squad, said: "California’s tenant protection laws serve an important purpose, but they can also create unintended challenges when individuals unlawfully occupy properties. In some situations, the legal framework makes it difficult for law enforcement to quickly distinguish between legitimate tenants and individuals who have no lawful right to occupy a property. When that distinction cannot be established immediately, property owners may be forced into lengthy and costly legal proceedings to regain possession of their own property. "The issue isn’t whether legitimate tenants deserve protection. They absolutely do. The issue is ensuring that those protections cannot be exploited by individuals who unlawfully occupy someone else’s property. We need a system that protects legitimate tenants while also providing property owners and law enforcement with a clear, efficient process for addressing unlawful occupancy." But in the end, we got the property back," Squatter Squad said. SEND US A TIP As for the homeowner – she is pleading with her state to make changes to stop this situation from happening. articles.title: Israeli court upholds detention of Palestinian land activist Ghassan Najjar
articles.summary: Occupied West Bank land defender is set to remain in detention until at least February 26 next year.
articles.body:
An Israeli military court has upheld a four–month administrative detention order against Palestinian land activist and farmer Ghassan Najjar.

Najjar appeared at Ofer Military Court on Monday. He was arrested during a pre–dawn raid on Burin village, south of Nablus, in the occupied West Bank on October 27, and has been held in administrative detention since.

The Israeli authorities have not given a reason for Najjar’s arrest, as administrative detention allows them. The Palestinian human rights defender, farmer and veteran grassroots organiser has a long history of arrest, having spent nearly a decade in Israeli prisons, much of it under administrative detention. He has been subjected to a travel ban since 2011.

The Institute for Middle East Understanding (IMEU) told Al Jazeera that Najjar was arrested because he intended to harvest olives on his land and planned to help other Palestinian farmers do the same. Israel’s security agency Shin Bet reportedly warned Najjar, cofounder of Burin’s Land and Farming Agricultural Cooperative, that he would be arrested if he did not stop organising with grassroots groups and Western activists.

The olive harvest in the occupied West Bank is a key target of pogroms by Israeli settlers. The attacks have surged during this year’s harvest and have already surpassed last year’s figures.

The United Nations and international voices have long urged Israel to guarantee Palestinian farmers’ protection and safe access to their land.

Administrative detention allows Israel to detain people without charge or trial, notes B’Tselem, an Israeli human rights group. It adds that the absence of legal proceedings leaves detainees “helpless”.

Following the court’s confirmation of the detention order, Najjar will remain in Ofer Prison until at least 26 February, his sister, Suha Najjar, told Al Jazeera. However, in the meantime, an Israeli military court will review his case and decide whether to extend the term.

“It is an unjust decision, and it is deeply upsetting that my brother has been subjected to such a great injustice,” Suha said.

“He has been placed under administrative detention for four months, without any charges [lodged] against him. Even more concerning is that this detention could be renewed when the four months come to an end.”

Earlier this month, Amnesty International demanded Israeli authorities release Najjar immediately. The rights group accused Israel of detaining him “solely because of his peaceful activism to protect the olive harvest season in Burin”.

“I am extremely worried, especially because we are not allowed to visit him or even see him. This makes our anxiety as a family even greater, as we have no way of knowing how he is doing, either physically or psychologically,” Suha said.

“We are aware of the cruel methods used by the Israeli occupation to torture Palestinian prisoners, both physically and psychologically, and this makes us even more fearful for his safety and wellbeing.”

In a statement released earlier this month, Amnesty called on states with leverage to pressure Israel to release Najjar.

“Like Palestinian human rights defender Ayman Bani Owda and countless other Palestinians, Ghassan Najjar is being hounded by a discriminatory justice system that has played a key role in legitimising and maintaining Israel’s system of apartheid and unlawful occupation,” it said.

“States with influence on Israel must use their leverage to pressure Israeli authorities into releasing all arbitrarily detained Palestinians, including Ghassan Najjar, and finally end their use of administrative detention.”

articles.title: Jensen Huang Resigns From Nvidia: Policy Issues Central to the Alleged Spying Scandal
articles.summary: Jensen Huang’s ouster from Nvidia raises questions about critical policy issues, including AI chip export enforcement and spying on U.S. companies.
articles.body: This article was originally published on CFR.org and updated by NBC News. U.S. chipmaking firm Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies in the world, announced the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday, November 12, days after its board said that it would launch an investigation into allegations that a Chinese espionage operation had targeted him. Nvidia said that Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will step in as interim CEO while the board begins a search for a permanent successor. It also named longtime director Harvey Jones the company’s first board chair.
